claims.text: HEA nanoparticles can be synthesized by low-temperature reduction of solid precursors.
Low-temperature solid-state reduction restricts free atomic diffusion during nanoparticle formation.
Restricted mobility during low-temperature reduction produces a kinetically trapped, highly disordered, high-entropy, strained lattice.
The kinetically trapped lattice preserves a near-equiatomic elemental distribution.
The kinetically trapped lattice inhibits phase segregation at high service temperatures.
The degree of mobility suppression during nanoparticle formation governs subsequent structural and chemical stability.
A post-synthesis anneal at 773 K permits additional atomic diffusion.
Anneal-enhanced mobility promotes local atomic ordering or phase segregation.
Increased ordering or segregation reduces lattice strain.
Unannealed nanoparticles will retain a uniform, single-phase structure during exposure to the stated service temperatures.
Annealed nanoparticles will exhibit more elemental segregation or phase formation than unannealed nanoparticles.
The unannealed nanoparticles will have superior catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Annealing-induced segregation will cause a decline in catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to HEA nanoparticles made from solid mixed precursors with limited atomic mobility.
Solution-based reduction routes have higher atomic mobility than solid-precursor reduction routes.
Different stabilization mechanisms may dominate in solution-based synthesis.
Prior observations support kinetic freezing of a high-entropy state in HEA nanoparticles.
The temperature threshold, diffusion activation energies, and required strain reduction for segregation have not been quantitatively determined.
No significant annealed-versus-unannealed difference in phase homogeneity, lattice strain, or performance would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The 773 K pre-anneal is asserted to activate mobility and segregation, but the nominally unannealed control is subsequently exposed to service temperatures beginning at 773 K and extending much higher. Without a specified difference in duration or thermal dose, the intervention does not cleanly separate mobility during annealing from mobility during service.

The hypothesis covers thermoelectric service up to 1923 K, whereas the described in situ test covers only 773–1173 K and evaluates a catalytic reaction. The stated experiment therefore cannot decisively falsify the thermoelectric-regime prediction across its full boundary.
